title: AI Foundry Lab
text:
Course Numbers
The BYU AI Foundry is an AI-native product studio and consultancy, and an official program of the BYU Marriott School of Business. We build AI products. One team works out what is worth building and then ships it, because those are no longer two jobs.
This site is the student program guide. It covers the course, how client teams are staffed, and the standard your work is held to. Everything a prospective client reads lives on the official website, aifoundry.byu.edu.
The Foundry is not an internship placement and not a research project. Every engagement ends with software running in the client’s hands, and a real company has paid for it.
There is no prerequisite. Many students take Build, IS 693R / MSB 341, first. Many take both classes in the same semester. What you have already shipped does not decide whether you are in the Foundry. It decides what you own on a team.
This course is cross-listed under two course numbers. It is all the same class: everyone meets together Fridays 8:00 to 11:50 AM in 2140 TNRB, works on the same client teams, uses this site, and is graded on the same rubric. Register under whichever number fits your program.
Mixed MBA and undergraduate teams are intentional. The MBAs bring the business judgment, the undergraduate builders bring engineering depth, and on a Foundry team those are the same job.

title: AI Foundry Lab
text:
How We Develop Builders
The Foundry trains full-stack product builders: people who can carry an idea from a user problem to a working product someone actually uses, with AI as both the material and the tool.
Two shapes describe that person.

The Builder is what you can make. Six axes: Discovery, Design, Application Architecture, AI Systems, Agentic Workflow, and Launch and Learn. Students self-report on all six at the start of fall semester and again in December, and see their own profile both times.
The Consultant is what changes when the work belongs to someone else. Four axes: Ownership, Client Presence, Communication, and Collaboration. These are not self-reported. Faculty and teammates rate them against observed behavior at midterm and at the end of the term.
Nobody arrives strong on all ten. Teams are staffed so the team covers every Builder axis even when no single member does.







Class
What it does




Build, IS 693R / MSB 341
Raises your floor. The goal is not a 5 anywhere, it is nothing below a 3


The Foundry Lab, this course
Tests your ceiling, and is the only place the Consultant axes develop at all

One engagement ships one product. 640 hours builds and ships one focused product. It does not build two. The team is small on purpose. Two builders with QC and faculty oversight riding on top is enough to ship something real and not enough to sprawl.

section: How Teams Are Staffed, in Short
text:
How Teams Are Staffed, in Short
Fit decides which projects you are eligible for. Points decide which eligible project you get.

One engagement, one pod: an engagement lead, two builders, a QC lead, and faculty oversight. A builder is on exactly one engagement at a time.
Six archetypes describe what a project needs and what you can do. A pod needs a rated 3 in the project’s primary archetype, plus a second 3 on the bench as backup.
100 points a month, capped at 300. Eligible builders bid sealed for the open seat. Second-highest bid sets the price, so bid your real level of interest.
The Foundry runs at most 6 concurrent engagements, with a seventh pod held in reserve. The binding constraint on how much work we take is builder hours, not demand.

Full rules: How Teams Are Staffed.

title: Syllabus
text:
What This Course Is
The AI Foundry is an AI-native product studio and consultancy. You are on a delivery team for a paying client. The client is paying a fixed fee, retains the intellectual property, and expects professional work. Your grade reflects both the quality of what you ship and the professionalism with which you ship it.
We ship, not advise. Discovery work is real and comes first, but it exists to point at something to build. Every engagement ends with software running in the client’s hands, not with a deck.
This is a two-semester course. You enroll each semester. Engagements are accepted on a rolling basis, so your team’s phase boundaries come from your kick-off rather than from a course-wide calendar.

How You Are Assessed
Two instruments run alongside the point total, and they measure different things in different ways.
The Builder, six axes: Discovery, Design, Application Architecture, AI Systems, Agentic Workflow, and Launch and Learn. You self-report these at the start of fall semester and again in December. They are not graded. They exist so you can see your own profile, so teams can be staffed for coverage, and so the program can tell whether the year moved you.
The Consultant, four axes: Ownership, Client Presence, Communication, and Collaboration. These are what changes when the work belongs to someone else, and they are not self-reported. The faculty advisor and your teammates rate them against observed behavior at midterm and at the end of each semester, using the same 1 to 5 scale with written behavioral anchors.
The Consultant ratings inform the Client Evaluation and Peer / Team Evaluation components below. They do not add points of their own.

title: Syllabus
text:
Confidentiality and Client Data
Foundry clients share confidential business information: financials, pipelines, customer data, and strategy. This is a condition of the work, and it carries obligations.

You will sign the client’s NDA, or the Foundry’s standard mutual NDA, before receiving data.
Client data stays in the approved project repository and approved tools. It does not go into personal accounts, personal cloud storage, or unapproved AI services.
Nothing about the project goes on LinkedIn, in a portfolio, or in a job interview without written client permission. Ask the faculty advisor first, every time.
Deliverables and intellectual property belong to the client, not to you and not to BYU.
When the project ends, you delete local copies of client data.

A confidentiality breach is an Honor Code matter and will also end the engagement. Treat this as the professional obligation it is.

title: Syllabus
text:
AI Use Policy
You are expected to use AI tools aggressively. That is the point of the Foundry. The obligations that come with it:

You own the output. “The model produced it” is not a defense for a wrong number, a fabricated citation, or an analysis you cannot explain.
Every deliverable must be explainable. If you cannot walk the client through why the model recommends what it recommends, it is not done.
Client data goes only into approved tools. See the confidentiality section above.
Disclose method, not apology. Milestone documentation should say what tools and models you used and how you validated the output.

title: Syllabus
text:
Instructor Bio
Scott Murff is an Associate Teaching Professor of Strategy at the BYU Marriott School of Business, where he also serves as faculty advisor and teaches courses on business strategy, decision-making, and artificial intelligence. He brings over 15 years of experience at the intersection of business and technology, having worked as a consultant, product manager, and data scientist.
Prior to joining BYU, Scott spent nearly seven years at McKinsey & Company in roles ranging from analytics specialist consultant to principal product manager, where he led product development and performance management initiatives for Fortune 500 clients. His earlier career includes building forecasting models as a VP at Zions Bancorporation and conducting regulatory research at the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Scott holds a Master’s degree in Management Science & Engineering from Stanford University and a B.A. in Economics with a minor in Math, from BYU. He is passionate about helping students apply AI, analytics, and strategy to meaningful real-world problems with both rigor and purpose.

Mission and Aims
The mission of Brigham Young University — founded, supported, and guided by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints: is to assist individuals in their quest for perfection and eternal life. That assistance should provide a period of intensive learning in a stimulating setting where a commitment to excellence is expected and the full realization of human potential is pursued.
BYU seeks to develop students of faith, intellect, and character who have the skills and the desire to continue learning and to serve others throughout their lives.
A BYU education should be (1) spiritually strengthening, (2) intellectually enlarging, and (3) character building, leading to (4) lifelong learning and service.
Building on the foundational Mission and Aims, the Marriott School of Business aspires to transform the world through Christlike leadership by developing leaders of faith, intellect, and character guided by the following 4 values:

Faith in Christ - We value deep and abiding faith in Jesus Christ. Our faith gives us the capacity to envision a better future, the confidence to make that future happen, and the courage to act in the face of challenges.
Integrity in Action - We value integrity and hold ourselves to the highest moral and ethical standards. Acting with integrity builds trust, strengthens character, and focuses our ambitions on things of eternal consequence.
Respect for All - We value respect for all individuals as children of God and recognize the inherent worth, divine potential, and agency of each person. A climate of respect and belonging enhances our learning, facilitates collaboration, and encourages personal growth.
Excellence - We value excellence in learning, teaching, research, management, and leadership. An expectation of excellence magnifies our influence and motivates us to continually improve.

We evaluate our decisions and actions by the impact they will have on the academic experience, professional preparation, character development, emotional well-being, and spiritual growth of our students.

title: Syllabus

Honor Code
In keeping with the principles of the BYU Honor Code, students are expected to be honest in all of their academic work. Academic honesty means, most fundamentally, that any work you present as your own must in fact be your own work and not that of another. Violations of this principle may result in a failing grade in the course and additional disciplinary action by the university. Students are also expected to adhere to the Dress and Grooming Standards. Adherence demonstrates respect for yourself and others and ensures an effective learning and working environment. It is the university’s expectation, and every instructor’s expectation in class, that each student will abide by all Honor Code standards. Please call the Honor Code Office at 422-2847 if you have questions about those standards.

Preventing & Responding to Sexual Misconduct
The health and well-being of students is of paramount importance at Brigham Young University. If you or someone you know has experienced sexual harassment (including sexual violence), there are many resources available for assistance.
In accordance with Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, BYU prohibits unlawful sex discrimination, including sexual harassment, against any participant in its education programs or activities. The university also prohibits sexual harassment by its personnel and students. Sexual harassment occurs when
a person is subjected to unwelcome sexual speech or conduct so severe, pervasive, and offensive that it effectively denies their ability to access any BYU education program or activity; any aid, benefit, or service of BYU is conditioned on a person’s participation in unwelcome sexual conduct; or a person suffers sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, or stalking on the basis of sex. University policy requires all faculty members to promptly report incidents of sexual harassment that come to their attention in any way, including through face-to-face conversations, a written class assignment or paper, class discussion, email, text, or social media post. Incidents of sexual harassment should be reported to the Title IX Coordinator at t9coordinator@byu.edu or (801) 422-8692 or 1085 WSC. Reports may also be submitted online at https://titleix.byu.edu/report or 1-888-238-1062 (24-hours a day).
BYU offers confidential resources for those affected by sexual harassment, including the university’s Sexual Assault Survivor Advocate, as well as a number of non-confidential resources and services that may be helpful. Additional information about Title IX, the university’s Sexual Harassment Policy, reporting requirements, and resources can be found at http://titleix.byu.edu or by contacting the university’s Title IX Coordinator.

Student Disability
Brigham Young University is committed to providing a working and learning atmosphere that reasonably accommodates qualified persons with disabilities. A disability is a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities. Whether an impairment is substantially limiting depends on its nature and severity, its duration or expected duration, and its permanent or expected permanent or long-term impact. Examples include vision or hearing impairments, physical disabilities, chronic illnesses, emotional disorders (e.g., depression, anxiety), learning disorders, and attention disorders (e.g., ADHD). If you have a disability which impairs your ability to complete this course successfully, please contact the University Accessibility Center (UAC), 2170 WSC or 801-422-2767 to request a reasonable accommodation. The UAC can also assess students for learning, attention, and emotional concerns. If you feel you have been unlawfully discriminated against on the basis of disability, please contact the Equal Opportunity Office at 801-422-5895, eo_manager@byu.edu, or visit https://hrs.byu.edu/equal-opportunity for help.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
The Pod
Client engagements are the course. This page is how you end up on one, and how you influence which one.
Two things decide it. Fit determines which projects you are eligible for. Points determine which eligible project you get. Fit is a gate, not a tiebreaker, and it always runs first.
One engagement, one pod. A pod is the smallest group that can find the problem, build the thing, and hand it over without a handoff inside the team.
The client pays for 640 builder hours across eight months. QC, design, and faculty time ride on top of that. This is why the one rule that never bends is that a builder is on exactly one engagement at a time. Your ten hours are sold.
Engagement lead owns the client relationship: the weekly call, the weekly update, the decision log, scope, and escalation. Owns the answer to “is this still inside 640 hours.”
Builder A is accountable for the architecture. Builder B is accountable for shipping alongside them. Both write code.
QC lead is a gate. Nothing reaches the client without passing it, and the review happens at kickoff and at every phase boundary, not the night before a milestone.
An engagement lead can carry two engagements. A QC lead can carry four. Builders carry one.

The Six Builder Archetypes
Every project gets classified at intake with a primary and a secondary archetype. Every builder carries a self-reported rating on all six, calibrated by faculty. This is the matching key.









Archetype
What it looks like in practice




A
Full-stack application
Net-new web or mobile app. Auth, database, deploy


B
AI and agents
LLM pipelines, scoring, evals, retrieval, agent orchestration


C
Data and modeling
Forecasting, optimization, analytics, decision frameworks


D
Integration and automation
APIs, webhooks, document processing, workflow glue


E
Product design
Design-heavy surfaces, design systems, net-new interfaces


F
Domain and strategy
Regulated industries, market analysis, business rules



Ratings run 0 to 3. 0 none. 1 coursework only. 2 you have shipped it once. 3 you can lead it and teach it.
These map onto the Builder hexagon from the program overview. The hexagon is about your development. The archetypes are about what a specific client is paying for this semester.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
The Matching Rule
A pod is validly staffed only when all four are true:

At least one builder is rated 3 in the project’s primary archetype.
The two builders together cover the secondary archetype at 2 or better.
Neither builder is on another active engagement.
Someone else on the bench, outside the pod, is also rated 3 in the primary archetype.

Rule 4 is the two-deep rule. It exists so that one person dropping the course does not end a client engagement. If we cannot satisfy rules 1 and 4, we do not sign the build phase. We sell discovery only, or we decline the project.
That is a real constraint on the kind of work the Foundry can take, and it is the honest reason some projects get turned down.

Any other use
None



The cap and the reset exist so the market is not decided by whoever has been idle longest. Sitting on the bench since September should be an advantage. It should not be an unbeatable one.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
The Auction

A new engagement signs. We post the project brief: what it is, primary and secondary archetype, risk tier, estimated hours, and the client’s industry.
The fit gate runs. We publish the eligible roster for that project. Eligibility is the matching rule plus being free of any other engagement. If you are not eligible, you cannot bid and you lose nothing.
Builder A is appointed, not auctioned. Faculty names the builder rated 3 in the primary archetype and confirms the two-deep backup.
Builder B is auctioned. Sealed bids from the eligible roster. One bid each, 72-hour window, no revisions.
Second price wins. The highest bid takes the seat and pays the second-highest bid plus one point. Everyone else pays nothing and keeps their balance.
Ties break toward the builder with fewer completed engagements, then by coin flip.
Results are published. Every bid and every clearing price, after the fact. You should be able to see what projects have historically cost.







Tip



Bid your actual level of interest. Second-price is not a gimmick. Because the winner pays the runner-up’s bid rather than their own, there is no advantage to shading your bid downward or trying to guess what everyone else will do. The strategy that wins is stating what the project is genuinely worth to you. If you find yourself doing game theory, you are working harder than the rules require.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
Guardrails
Fit is never overridden by points. A large bid from an ineligible builder is not a bid. The client is paying for the right team, and enthusiasm does not substitute for the skill they are buying.
Nobody sits out a semester. If you have zero engagements by the midpoint of the term, you get a directed placement into the next opening, outside the auction. The market allocates enthusiasm. It does not decide who gets to participate.
Some projects are closed to the auction. Engagements involving regulated data, records about minors, or systems that influence decisions about people are staffed by appointment. There are not many of these, and you will know which ones they are because the brief says so.
Faculty veto exists. It gets used rarely and it gets explained when it does.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
Discovery Teams
A discovery-only engagement is not a full pod. It is an engagement lead plus one builder, four to six weeks, and its job is to find out whether the real project fits in 640 hours.
If the build phase then signs, the builder who ran discovery gets first claim on the Builder A seat without bidding. The context they built is worth more than the scheduling convenience of reopening it.
Discovery is the fastest route onto a project you care about. It costs no points.

title: How Teams Are Staffed
text:
What This Means for You

Your archetype ratings decide your eligibility, so raise the low ones. The fastest way to become eligible for more projects is to ship something in an archetype where you are a 1.
Being a 3 in something matters more than being a 2 in everything. Rule 1 asks for a specialist. Rule 4 means we need two of them.
Spend points on the project you actually want. Hoarding to 300 and never bidding is the one strategy that is strictly dominated.
Take a discovery slot if one is open. It is a free option on the build seat.

title: Weekly Updates
text:
Deadline
Every team sends one end-of-week progress email. It keeps the client informed, creates a record of the engagement, and is worth 28% of your grade.
Saturday by 11:59 PM
The end-of-week timing is intentional. It forces reflection on what actually got done, sets priorities before Monday, and surfaces blockers while there is still time to fix them.

title: Weekly Updates
text:
First weekly email due: September 5, 2026
Final weekly email due: April 10, 2027
Total weekly emails: 28 (14 per semester)

title: Weekly Updates
text:
Who Sends It
The client lead sends one email on behalf of the team. Individual students do not each send their own. If the client lead is unavailable, the QC lead sends it. Missing an email is a team-level miss, and everyone takes the point deduction.

title: Weekly Updates
text:
Recipients

To: Client point of contact
CC: aifoundry@byu.edu, plus all team members

title: Weekly Updates
text:
Email Format
1. Accomplished this week [Required]

Completed work and deliverables, stated as outcomes rather than activities
Include the number, the finding, or the decision, not just “worked on the model”

2. Priorities for next week [Required]

What the team will do, realistically
Who owns each item

3. Decisions or input we need from you [Required, say “none” if none]

Anything the client owes the team
Any decision the team cannot make on the client’s behalf

4. Blockers, risks, or dependencies [Omit if none]

Anything that puts a milestone at risk
Flag it the week you see it, not the week it hits

title: Weekly Updates
text:
Example Email
Subject: AI Foundry Weekly Update - [Client] - Week of Oct 5

Hi [Name],

Accomplished this week:
- Scored 42 of the 60 candidate products against the draft criteria. 11 clear
  the NPV multiple threshold of 3.0x under base-case assumptions.
- Reconciled the revenue baseline to your FY26 actuals. We were off by 2.3%
  on specialty; the gap was a channel mapping issue, now corrected.
- Drafted the sensitivity structure for price erosion and launch timing.

Priorities for next week:
- Finish scoring the remaining 18 products (Maria, Josh)
- Run the first full sensitivity pass and identify which rankings are fragile (Ana)
- Draft the discovery findings document for your review (Tyler)

Decisions or input we need from you:
- Confirm whether the 12% price erosion assumption should hold across all
  therapeutic areas or vary by category. This changes the ranking materially.
- We need read access to the 2024-2025 gross-to-net detail to validate margin.

Risks:
- If the gross-to-net data is not available in the next week, discovery will
  land with modeled margin rather than actuals, and we will need to revisit the
  build estimate afterward.

Thanks,
[Client lead name], on behalf of the [Client] Foundry team

title: Weekly Updates
text:
What Makes an Update Good

Lead with the number or the finding. “11 of 42 products clear the threshold” beats “continued portfolio scoring.”
Name owners. Unowned priorities do not get done.
Ask for what you need explicitly. Clients cannot read minds, and a blocker you did not raise is your fault, not theirs.
Flag risk early and unemotionally. A risk raised in week 4 is a conversation. The same risk surfaced in week 12 is a failure.
Never pad. A short honest week is fine. A long week of activity with no outcomes is not.

title: Build Standards
text:
The Four Dimensions
Milestones are graded against these standards. They are also what separates work a client pays for from work a client tolerates.
Every deliverable is scored on correctness, usefulness, explainability, and craft.

title: Build Standards
text:
Correctness

Code does what it claims. If it is shipped, it has been run against something real
Every number in a client-facing document traces to a source you can point to
Totals reconcile. If your revenue baseline is 2% off the client’s actuals, you find out why before you present it, not after they do
Assumptions are written down as assumptions, with the value used and the reason for it
If you do not know something, the deliverable says so. Fabricated precision is worse than an honest range



Usefulness

Someone at the client would actually open it. A tool nobody uses is a failed deliverable
It solves the problem the client actually has, integrated with the systems they actually run
Discovery output names specific things to build, with an estimate and a sequence, not themes
Scope creep is not usefulness. If the client’s question changed, renegotiate it in writing



Explainability
This is the standard the Foundry is built around, and it is where AI-assisted work most often fails.

For any model output, you can state which inputs drove it and by how much
Rankings come with sensitivity: what would have to change for the order to change
A model no one on the team can explain is not shippable, regardless of how good the output looks
“The model said so” is never an answer to a client question



Craft

The repository is clean, has a README, and someone outside the team could run it
Tests exist where breakage would be expensive. Not everywhere, but not nowhere
Deployment is documented and repeatable, not a thing one person knows how to do
Documents are proofread. Charts are labeled. Slides have a point per slide
No client data in personal accounts, personal repos, or unapproved tools

title: Build Standards
text:
Repository Standards
Every engagement has one private repository in the ai-foundry-byu GitHub organization, named client-<slug>.
client-<slug>/
  README.md          What this is, how to run it, how to deploy it, who to ask
  discovery/         The audit: findings, what to build, estimates, sequence
  app/               The application. Whatever stack the job calls for
  integrations/      Connections into the client's systems
  analysis/          Notebooks and scripts, in order, that reproduce every number
  deliverables/      What the client actually receives, versioned by milestone
  docs/              Handoff docs, meeting notes, decision log, scope changes
Two rules that are not negotiable:

No secrets or client data in the repository. Ever. Credentials live in the client’s own systems or an approved secret store.
Every number in a deliverable is reproducible from something in analysis/. If you cannot rerun it, you cannot defend it.

title: Build Standards
text:
The Decision Log
Keep docs/decisions.md current. One entry per material decision:
2026-10-09: Price erosion assumption
Decision: Use 12% annual erosion for specialty, 18% for hospital, rather than a
flat 15% across the portfolio.
Why: Client's 2023-2025 actuals show materially different curves by channel.
Who: Confirmed with Brian Guy on the Oct 8 call.
Reversible: Yes. Sensitivity range 8-22% is built into the model.
This is the single highest-leverage habit in the course. It is what lets you answer “why did you assume that” six months later, and it is what makes handoff possible.

title: Build Standards
text:
QC Gate
Nothing goes to the client without the QC lead’s sign-off. The QC lead checks:

It runs. Someone other than the author has run it from a clean checkout
Every number traces to a source, and totals reconcile against the client’s own figures
Assumptions are stated, with values and reasons
Model outputs are explainable in plain language
Deployment steps are written down and have been followed once by someone else
No client data or secrets in the repository
Document is proofread, charts are labeled, filenames are clean

A milestone that fails QC after it reaches the client costs the whole team craft points. Catch it internally.

title: Build Standards
text:
Working with AI
Use AI tools hard. They are why a team of five can deliver what used to take fifteen.

Generate freely, verify always. Treat every model output as a draft from a fast, capable, occasionally confident-and-wrong analyst.
Check citations and figures by hand. Fabricated sources have ended real consulting engagements.
Keep client data out of unapproved tools. See the confidentiality terms in the Syllabus.
Document your method. Milestone documentation should state which tools you used, for what, and how you validated the output. This is not a confession, it is methodology.
